guide.summary: Unit 8 covers chi-square tests for categorical data: goodness of fit (one variable vs. a claimed distribution), homogeneity (comparing distributions across several populations or treatments), and independence (association between two variables in one population). You must pick the right test, compute expected counts, check conditions, and interpret results.

sections.heading: Choosing the test
sections.body: Goodness of fit (GOF): one categorical variable from one sample, compared with a hypothesized distribution (e.g., is a die fair?). Homogeneity: one categorical variable measured on samples from two or more populations or treatment groups (separate samples). Independence: two categorical variables measured on a single sample (one sample, classified two ways). The calculations for homogeneity and independence are identical; the difference is in how the data were collected and how hypotheses are stated.

sections.heading: Hypotheses and expected counts
sections.body: GOF: H₀: the stated proportions are correct (list them); Hₐ: at least one proportion differs. Homogeneity: H₀: the distribution of [variable] is the same for all populations; Hₐ: the distributions are not all the same. Independence: H₀: there is no association between [var 1] and [var 2] (they are independent); Hₐ: there is an association. Expected counts: GOF: n × hypothesized proportion. Two-way tables: (row total × column total)/grand total. Expected counts need not be whole numbers.

sections.heading: Conditions and calculations
sections.body: Conditions: Random (random sample(s) or random assignment); 10% when sampling without replacement; Large Counts: all expected counts ≥ 5. Test statistic: χ² = Σ(observed − expected)²/expected, always using counts, never percentages. df: GOF = number of categories − 1; two-way table = (rows − 1)(columns − 1). χ² distributions are right-skewed; the P-value is the upper-tail area. Larger χ² means larger discrepancy from H₀. To find which categories contributed most, compare individual components (O − E)²/E and say whether observed was above or below expected.

sections.heading: Interpreting results
sections.body: If P ≤ α, there is convincing evidence for Hₐ (a different distribution or an association); if P > α, there is not convincing evidence. Chi-square tests never show the direction or strength of an association on their own; follow up by comparing conditional proportions or the largest components. An association in observational data is not causation.

keyTakeaways: GOF: one variable, one sample, claimed distribution.
Homogeneity: several samples; independence: one sample, two variables.
commonMistakes: Checking observed counts (not expected) for the ≥ 5 condition.
Claiming a chi-square test proves causation.
examTips: Name the test exactly and justify by describing the sampling design.
Show at least one expected count calculation.
Identify the largest contributor and describe its direction.
MCQs often ask which test fits a scenario or what df is.
guide.cramSheet:
**Tests:** GOF (1 var, claimed %) · homogeneity (≥ 2 samples) · independence (1 sample, 2 vars)

**Expected:** GOF n·p · table R·C/N

**Conditions:** Random · 10% · all expected ≥ 5

**χ²:** Σ(O − E)²/E · counts only · right-skewed · upper tail

**df:** k − 1 · (r − 1)(c − 1)

**Follow-up:** biggest (O − E)²/E and direction

vocab.definition: Σ(observed − expected)²/expected; measures how far observed counts are from expected counts.
Tests whether one categorical variable's distribution matches a hypothesized distribution.
Tests whether the distribution of a categorical variable is the same across several populations or treatments.
Tests whether two categorical variables are associated in one population.
The count predicted for a cell if H₀ were true.
The actual count in each category or cell.
k − 1 for GOF; (rows − 1)(columns − 1) for two-way tables.
A single term (O − E)²/E of the chi-square statistic.
A right-skewed distribution used for χ² P-values; shape depends on df.
All expected counts are at least 5.
A table of counts classified by two categorical variables.
A relationship in which knowing one variable's value changes the distribution of the other.

practice.topic: 8.6 Carrying Out a Chi-Square Test for Homogeneity or Independence
practice.stem: A chi-square test for independence between age group and preferred social media platform yields χ² = 11.2 with df = 4. Which conclusion is correct at α = 0.05?

choices.text: P ≈ 0.024; there is convincing evidence of an association between age group and preferred platform.
P ≈ 0.024; age causes platform preference.
P ≈ 0.976; no association.
P ≈ 0.12; no convincing evidence of an association.

practice.explanation: Upper-tail area for χ² = 11.2, df = 4 is about 0.024 < 0.05.

practice.topic: 8.5 Setting Up a Chi-Square Test for Homogeneity or Independence

practice.topic: 8.6 Carrying Out a Chi-Square Test for Homogeneity or Independence
practice.stem: If every count in a two-way table were doubled (same proportions, twice the sample size), what would happen to χ² and the P-value?

choices.text: Both stay the same.
χ² doubles and the P-value decreases.
χ² is halved and the P-value increases.
χ² quadruples and df doubles.

practice.explanation: Each (O − E)² quadruples while E doubles, so each component doubles; df is unchanged.

practice.topic: 8.3 Carrying Out a Chi-Square Test for Goodness of Fit
practice.stem: A student runs a chi-square test using percentages (e.g., 34%, 41%, 25%) instead of counts from a sample of 1,000. What is the effect?

choices.text: No effect, because proportions are equivalent to counts.
χ² is computed on the wrong scale; with n = 1,000, it would be 10 times too small, inflating the P-value.
χ² would be too large.
The degrees of freedom would change.

practice.explanation: Percent values are counts divided by 10 here; χ² scales with counts, so it shrinks by a factor of 10.

practice.topic: 8.6 Carrying Out a Chi-Square Test for Homogeneity or Independence
practice.stem: A chi-square test for homogeneity comparing satisfaction (low/medium/high) across three hospitals gives P = 0.003. The largest component is for Hospital C, 'low' (observed 48, expected 30). Which follow-up statement is best?

choices.text: Hospital C had more low-satisfaction patients than expected if the distributions were the same, contributing most to the evidence of a difference.
Hospital C caused low satisfaction.
All hospitals differ from one another in every category.
Hospital C had fewer low-satisfaction patients than expected.

practice.explanation: Observed exceeds expected in the largest contributing cell.

distractors.C: The test says the distributions aren't all the same, not that every pair differs.

practice.topic: 8.5 Setting Up a Chi-Square Test for Homogeneity or Independence
practice.stem: In a randomized experiment, 300 patients are randomly assigned to three treatments, and each patient's outcome is recorded as improved, unchanged, or worse. Which analysis is appropriate, and what conclusion type is possible?

choices.text: Chi-square test for homogeneity; if significant, treatments cause differences in outcome distributions.
Chi-square test for independence; only association can be concluded.
Goodness of fit; outcomes are compared with 1/3 each.
Two-sample t-test on outcomes.

practice.explanation: Treatment groups are compared on one categorical response; random assignment supports causation.

practice.topic: 8.6 Carrying Out a Chi-Square Test for Homogeneity or Independence
practice.prompt:
A random sample of 300 students at a large high school was asked whether they play a varsity sport and which new lunch option they prefer.

| | Option A | Option B | Option C | Total |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Athlete | 50 | 40 | 30 | 120 |
| Non-athlete | 50 | 70 | 60 | 180 |
| Total | 100 | 110 | 90 | 300 |

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify the appropriate test and state the hypotheses.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the expected count for athletes who prefer Option A, and verify the Large Counts condition.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: The test statistic is χ² ≈ 6.44. Find the P-value and state a conclusion at α = 0.05.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Identify the cell that contributes most to χ² and describe what it shows.

rubric.description: Chi-square test for independence (one random sample, two variables). H₀: no association between athlete status and lunch preference among students at the school; Hₐ: there is an association.
(120)(100)/300 = 40; smallest expected count is (120)(90)/300 = 36 ≥ 5, so all are ≥ 5.
df = (2 − 1)(3 − 1) = 2; P ≈ 0.040 < 0.05: reject H₀; convincing evidence of an association between athlete status and lunch preference.
Athletes, Option A: (50 − 40)²/40 = 2.5; more athletes preferred Option A than expected under independence.

practice.sampleResponse:
(a) Chi-square test for independence, since one random sample of students was classified by two categorical variables.
H₀: There is no association between being a varsity athlete and lunch preference for students at this school.
Hₐ: There is an association between being a varsity athlete and lunch preference for students at this school.

(b) Expected (athlete, Option A) = (120 × 100)/300 = 40. The smallest expected count is (120 × 90)/300 = 36, so all expected counts are at least 5.

(c) df = (2 − 1)(3 − 1) = 2. P-value = P(χ² ≥ 6.44) ≈ 0.040. Since 0.040 < 0.05, we reject H₀. There is convincing evidence of an association between athlete status and lunch preference among students at this school.

(d) The athlete / Option A cell contributes most: (50 − 40)²/40 = 2.5. Athletes chose Option A more often than would be expected if athlete status and lunch preference were independent.
